title: From Single Spins to Ensembles: A Calibrated Symbolic Regression Pipeline for NV Spectroscopy
authors: Evan Zhang, Zhenghang Zhi, Zewei Wang, Zeheng Wang
abstract: Characterizing nitrogen-vacancy (NV) ensembles requires connecting their collective spectra to individual centers that experience different local environments. We develop a symbolic-regression pipeline that carries single-center spin structure into a calibrated ensemble model by generating individual spectral responses and combining them with explicit weights. A constrained search selects Hermitian operator terms from single-center optically detected magnetic resonance spectra, fits their coefficients, and retains the selected expressions as source models for the ensemble. Ensemble calibration then accounts for resonance shifts, local disorder, orientation, and optical response while keeping the individual spectral contributions accessible. On public single-center and ensemble data, the zero-field ensemble held-frequency root-mean-square error decreases from 0.008835 to 0.003872 in normalized photoluminescence, a 56.2% improvement over matched uncorrected composition. In controlled QuTiP ensembles of 128 sites spanning four NV orientations, models calibrated at 0 and 3 mT predict an independently held-out 5.17 mT spectrum with errors of 0.000207-0.000228 across three random seeds, comparable to the 0.000200 noise standard deviation. Resolving the simulated response into its individual-center contributions shows how local spectral diversity combines into the ensemble line shape. By retaining the source Hamiltonians while calibrating sample-dependent spectral differences, the pipeline connects local spin physics to collective optical readout and makes the contributions to an ensemble line shape available for physical interpretation.
summary: This paper introduces a symbolic regression pipeline to bridge the gap between single-spin physics and ensemble spectroscopy in NV centers. By treating the ensemble spectrum as a weighted sum of local responses, the method calibrates for disorder and local variations. This allows researchers to interpret the collective line shape by understanding the underlying contributions from individual, locally distinct spins.
main_problem: The core challenge is connecting the local spin physics observed in single Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers to the complex, collective spectral response measured from an ensemble of centers experiencing varied local environments.
main_result: The developed pipeline significantly improves the prediction accuracy of the ensemble spectrum, achieving up to a 56.2% reduction in the zero-field held-frequency RMSE compared to uncorrected models.
method: The authors developed a symbolic-regression pipeline that uses constrained search to derive single-center spin Hamiltonians and then calibrates these source models to account for ensemble-specific shifts and disorder.
model_or_system: The system is NV centers in diamond, whose collective behavior is modeled as a weighted sum of individual local spectral responses derived from an effective ground-state spin Hamiltonian. The model incorporates local disorder, orientation, and optical response.
key_observables: Zero-field and finite-field ensemble held-frequency root-mean-square error (RMSE); individual spectral contributions; ODMR spectra.
important_parameters: Applied magnetic fields (e.g., 0, 3, 5.17 mT); spectral shifts and disorder parameters; source hyperfine couplings.
main_assumptions: The ensemble spectrum is assumed to be a weighted sum of individual local spectra, allowing the separation of local operator determination from sample-specific calibration.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NV structure and spin levels, the calibrated pathway showing symbolic regression and source inheritance, and comparisons of RMSE reduction across different field conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical problem (local to ensemble), detailing the symbolic regression methodology (constrained search, coefficient fitting), presenting the calibration procedure (accounting for shifts/disorder), and validating the results using both public data and controlled QuTiP simulations.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, data-driven framework for extracting underlying physical Hamiltonians from complex, noisy ensemble measurements, which is highly relevant for characterizing disordered quantum materials.
